subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Anchoring Effect
description: A fast breakdown of The Anchoring Effect for builders.

hook.text: Spin a wheel that lands on 65. Now guess what percent of UN countries are African. You'll guess high.

buildup.text: Anchoring means the first number you see pulls your estimate toward it—even if it's totally random.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed anchors distort judgment even when people know the anchor is irrelevant.

twist.text: Retail pricing exploits this daily. A $500 jacket next to a $200 one makes the $200 one seem cheap.

climax.text: In salary talks, whoever names a number first sets the anchor. The whole negotiation orbits that point.

punchline.text: The first number wins. Choose it carefully.

quiz.question: What is the anchoring effect?
options: Initial numbers pull estimates toward them
People always choose the middle option

details.summary: The anchoring effect causes people to rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making judgments. Even random or irrelevant numbers influence subsequent estimates, because the initial anchor creates a starting point that adjustments fail to move far enough from.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring shapes negotiations, pricing, sentencing decisions, and everyday estimates. Awareness of this bias is the first step toward reducing its powerful influence on judgment.
takeaways: First information encountered disproportionately influences judgment
Even irrelevant anchors affect subsequent numerical estimates
Adjustment from anchors is typically insufficient

faq.question: Can knowing about anchoring prevent its effects?
faq.answer: Awareness helps somewhat but does not eliminate anchoring. Studies show that even experts who know about the bias are still influenced by anchors. The most effective strategy is to generate your own anchor independently before encountering external information.

faq.question: How is anchoring used in negotiations?
faq.answer: The first offer in a negotiation serves as a powerful anchor. Research shows that starting high as a seller or low as a buyer influences the final price significantly. Making the first offer is often advantageous because it sets the reference point for all subsequent discussion.
